title: Come, Lord Jesus (Apocalypse 22:17–21)
carry: take the water of life, freely
last: BEHOLD, I MAKE ALL THINGS NEW.

lines: THE LAST PAGE OF THE LIBRARY.
cards: Back on day three hundred thirty-two, a library opened at its first page: in the beginning. Since then, kings, prophets, psalms, Gospels, letters and visions. Today, the last page.
And the Bible doesn't end with a summary, or a moral, or a final warning. It ends with a conversation. Someone says come.
Someone answers I'm coming. And then the last prayer in the whole book, three words long. An older form of it turns up in one of Paul's letters, in another language.

teach.h: THE SPIRIT AND THE BRIDE SAY: COME.
teach.b: First, in the Douay-Rheims: "And the spirit and the bride say: Come. And he that heareth, let him say: Come." The Spirit and the bride, the Church, call out to Christ.
Then the invitation turns toward anyone listening: let him that thirsts come, and take the water of life, freely. Come goes both ways.
Then Christ answers: "Surely I come quickly: Amen. Come, Lord Jesus." That's the Bible's last prayer. Now back to Paul.
Writing in Greek to the Corinthians, he leaves one Aramaic word untranslated: maranatha. Aramaic was the language of Jesus and his first followers in Galilee.
Paul keeps the word the way you'd keep a word from a grandmother's language, because no other word feels right.
Scholars discuss two readings: maran atha, our Lord has come; or marana tha, our Lord, come! Christians can pray both. He has come; come again.
An early Christian handbook called the Didache puts maranatha in its prayers after the Eucharist, and come, Lord Jesus sounds, to some scholars, like that same old prayer put into Greek.
Then the Bible ends with a blessing: "The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you all. Amen."

teach.h: PRAYED AT EVERY MASS AND IN ADVENT.
teach.b: Catholics pray this longing at every Mass: after the Lord's Prayer, the priest prays for the people as they wait in hope for the coming of our Savior.
And all through Advent, the Church sings come. The book whose first page has God saying let there be light ends with his people saying come.

how: Catholics voice this longing at every Mass, in the prayer after the Lord's Prayer that speaks of waiting for the coming of the Savior, and especially in Advent, the season of preparing for Christ's coming; some pray maranatha as a short, repeated prayer.

o: Greek: the grace of the Lord be with you all
Hebrew: blessed is he who comes in God's name
Aramaic: our Lord, come, or our Lord has come

games.q: the last page — tap the pairs.

s: the Bible's last words are a warning
the last prayer is come, Lord Jesus, and the last verse is a blessing of grace.

scholars agree on exactly how to divide maranatha

games.q: you're writing the very last lines of the Bible. after all the visions, how do you end?
o: with a summary of everything that came before.
with a prayer, come, Lord Jesus, and a blessing of grace.
with a list of what's still to happen.
games.why: the Apocalypse ends with a conversation: the Spirit and the bride say come, Christ says I come quickly, and the people answer: Amen. come, Lord Jesus.

practice: Think of what in your life, or in the world, most needs to be made new, a sorrow, an illness, a war, a relationship, and hold it gently.

If you pray, say the Bible's last prayer on each out-breath, come, Lord Jesus, or the old Aramaic word, maranatha, until it's almost a whisper. If you don't, just feel what it's like to long for something to come.

wordCard.voice: Maranatha. Aramaic, from the first Christians: our Lord, come, or our Lord has come. The Bible's last prayer. Today's word.

orig.note: Aramaic words written in Greek letters (1 Corinthians 16:22): our Lord, come.

carryVoice: Your line: take the water of life, freely. And that's the Apocalypse: an unveiling, the first and the last, first charity, not lukewarm, the knock, holy, the Lamb, every tongue, the woman, Babylon, the supper, tabernacle, and maranatha. The last page, turned.
